segments.text: Welcome to your first chapter. Let's meet Eat Better Co, a healthy snacking brand from Jaipur, started in 2020.
Eat Better makes snacks people already love, like sweets, namkeens, and seed and nut mixes, but with better ingredients. Its promise is simple: snacks you love, ingredients you trust.
In the video, the founders tell the story in their own words: how the brand began, and what it stands for.

Eat Better is an internet-first brand. That means it sells directly to customers through its own website, instead of depending only on shops and distributors. This is called D2C, or direct to consumer, and it lets the brand hear from customers directly.
On the shelves you will find laddoos and sweets, namkeens, nut mixes, and gift boxes, each made with real ingredients.
Here is the big idea to remember. Eat Better started as a family kitchen and became a national brand by selling online. That is why we call it an internet-first brand.
In this chapter we learn what Eat Better stands for. Its philosophy is better ingredients, better quality, and better for you.

The vision is where the brand wants to go: to become India's most loved family snacking brand. The mission is what it does every day to get there: to revive the Indian snacking category with healthier, tastier options for every household.
Three values sit behind every snack the brand makes, and you can see them in its ingredients, its quality checks and its products.
A vision only matters when it guides real decisions. Each idea is checked against it: does this help us make snacks that are both tasty and better for you?
Finally, we look at what Eat Better sells, and the places where customers can buy it.
Remember this: a good vision is a filter. If a decision does not help the brand make snacks that are tasty and better for you, the answer is no.
Every brand starts with a problem. Eat Better began with a family that wanted snacks that were tasty and healthy at the same time.
Before selling online, the founders sold at exhibitions and through direct selling. At a stall, they could talk to customers, let them taste the snacks, and learn what they liked.
Step by step, the brand grew from one city to customers across India.
The three founders are Mridula Kanoria, Shaurya Kanoria and Vidushi Kajaria.
In the early days, the founders did everything themselves: making, selling and answering customers. As the company grew, each leader could focus on doing one thing really well.
Here is the lesson. The founders did not start with a big factory. They started with a real family problem, tested recipes with real customers, and scaled step by step.
This chapter asks a big question: does the product really solve a real problem?
The problem is that many snacks force people to choose between taste and health. Eat Better's answer is snacks that people love, made with better ingredients.
In the expedition, you become a consumer researcher. You listen to what people say, and also watch what they actually do, to find the real problem.
The table puts it all together: each problem, Eat Better's answer, and the proof.
So how do we know the fit is real? Fit is proven by repeat customers, not by advertising. Reviews, repeat orders and family-size packs are the real signals.
Eat Better makes four kinds of products: sweets and laddoos, namkeens, nuts and mixes, and combos and gifting.
Each one fits a different moment: daily snacking, festivals, gifting, and corporate orders.
In the innovation studio, you get to develop a new snack idea, the way a product team would.
Then you plan a family's whole snacking year, from everyday snacks to festive hampers.
The big idea: Eat Better's portfolio covers three habits, everyday snacking, festive sweets and gifting. That is how one brand can serve a family all year.
For a food brand, trust is everything. Eat Better's quality promise has six checkpoints that every batch must pass.
In the 3D facility, you become a quality specialist and check snacks before they are packed and sent out.
A clean label means short ingredient lists that people can actually read, with no palm oil, no refined sugar and no artificial preservatives. Snacks are sweetened with dates and dry fruits instead.
Food rules matter too. Products follow FSSAI requirements, are lab tested, and carry clear labels.
And the pack does important jobs, like keeping snacks fresh and crunchy until they reach you. Remember: for a food brand, trust is the product.

A brand is more than its snacks. In this chapter we look at six parts of a brand identity: the brand name, the logo and visual identity, colours, packaging, the brand's voice and tone, and how customers see it.
The name Eat Better, and the tagline, the joy of snacking made better, tell you the promise in just a few words. Colours, pack design and a friendly voice make the brand easy to recognise and trust.
In the Brand Identity Lab, you audit a real Eat Better pack in 3D: spot the identity on the pack, test colours, tune the brand's voice, and win over shoppers.
Finally, think about what would make you pick up a pack, and why. That is brand identity at work.
Eat Better's marketing started by listening. At exhibitions, the team met customers, heard their feedback, and improved the products.
Today the brand also talks to customers through channels it controls, like its website, email and blog.
On social media, one brand appears on four platforms: Instagram, YouTube, Facebook and LinkedIn.
Stories help too. The founders' story and behind-the-scenes videos build trust.
Reviews and ratings help new buyers decide, and offers like combos and free shipping give people a reason to buy today.

And customers can find the snacks in many places, from the brand's own website to marketplaces and quick commerce apps. Remember: for a D2C brand, marketing is not just ads. It is stories, reviews, community and a great first order that earns the second.

Brand positioning is the place a brand holds in a customer's mind. Eat Better aims to sit between traditional indulgent snacks and products sold mainly on health: familiar snacks with a better-for-you approach.
A target audience is the group a brand wants to reach. Eat Better speaks to health-conscious families, working professionals, festive gift buyers and corporate buyers.
A unique selling proposition is the reason to choose a brand. A strong one is specific, relevant, different from competitors, and backed by evidence.
A customer persona is a simple profile of a typical customer: who they are, what they need, and what makes them buy.
In the activities, you map where brands stand, check claims with evidence, and build a persona from real interviews.

2.4.title: Shark Tank India, PR and Campaigns

segments.text: This chapter is about attention the brand earned, not bought. It starts with national TV.
On Shark Tank India season four, the founders pitched Eat Better to a national audience and secured fifty lakh rupees.
Funding news builds trust too. Eat Better raised seventeen crore rupees in a Pre-Series A round, co-led by Prath Ventures and Spring Marketing Capital.
Festivals like Rakhi and Diwali bring big moments for healthier gift hampers.
Corporate gifting brings big clients, and big clients bring more trust.
Finally, the brand shows its press features on its own website. Remember: PR is earned attention, built on a strong story, clear standards and a product people trust.
The Business Model Canvas is a one-page map of how a business works. In this chapter we study its people side: four blocks about customers.
Customer segments are the groups a business serves. For Eat Better, that includes health-conscious families, young professionals and students, gift buyers, and corporate buyers.
The value proposition is the promise: familiar Indian taste, made with cleaner ingredients.
Channels are how a product reaches people: the brand's own website, marketplaces, quick commerce apps, and corporate orders.

And customer relationships are how the brand keeps people coming back, through reviews, customer care, offers and community. Remember: the people side of the canvas is about who customers are, what they need, and how you stay in touch.
This chapter opens the engine room of the business: three more blocks of the canvas.
Key resources are what the company must have, like its kitchen and production facility, its recipes and know-how, its team, and its brand.
Key activities are what it must do every day: source and check ingredients, cook and test, pack and fulfil orders, market the brand, and develop new products.
Key partners are who it depends on: ingredient suppliers, marketplaces and quick commerce apps, logistics and delivery partners, investors, and corporate clients.
Remember: these blocks show what the company must be good at, and who it needs on its side.
Now we reach the money side of the canvas: revenue streams and cost structure.
Revenue streams are the ways money comes in, like sales on the brand's website, on marketplaces and quick commerce apps, and corporate gifting orders.
The cost structure is where money goes out: ingredients, packaging, logistics, marketing, and the team and kitchen.

Profit is what is left when money in is bigger than money out. Eat Better's sales grew fast, from about five and a half crore rupees to about fourteen point seven crore rupees, while the business was still working towards profit.
Remember: growth and profit are different things. A brand can grow fast and still be working towards profitability.
This chapter is about where the snack meets the road: how products travel from the kitchen to you.
Eat Better reaches people through four pillars: its own website, marketplaces, quick commerce, and corporate and bulk orders.
Each route has its own speed. A website order can take a few days, while quick commerce can deliver in minutes from a nearby dark store.
Four things can go wrong on the way: snacks losing freshness, stock in the wrong place, big festival rushes, and high delivery costs.
Remember: great snacks do not matter if they arrive late, broken or stale. Logistics is part of the product.
To compare snack prices fairly, we look at the price for one gram. Divide the price by the grams, and you can compare a small box with a big one.
Three things change what a gram costs: the ingredients, a clean-label promise, and buying in bigger multi-packs.

The reported numbers show fast growth. Sales rose from about five and a half crore rupees to about fourteen point seven crore rupees, with about two lakh orders a month, while the business still made a loss.
Remember: pricing tells a story. A higher price per gram must be matched by a clearly better product, honest ingredients and a brand people trust.
Eat Better is not the only snack seller. This chapter compares it with traditional snack brands, health-snack competitors and local sweet shops.
A K-Matrix shows who is strong at what. It rates each player High, Medium or Low on the things customers choose by.
Eat Better's unique edge is natural sweetening, with dates and dry fruits. Its gap is mass-market price, where traditional brands are cheaper.
The chapter also compares Eat Better with five named health-snack brands, side by side.
For each rival, there is one place where Eat Better stands out. Remember: an edge or a gap only shows up when you compare across the same row.
After its Pre-Series A round in April 2025, Eat Better's management set out how it would grow.
The plan has four growth pillars: more products, deeper quick commerce reach, corporate and business gifting all year, and a bigger kitchen with more production capacity.
Each pillar changes different blocks of the Business Model Canvas, such as the value proposition, channels and key resources.
In the activities, you run parts of the plan yourself: expanding into new cities and planning the factory floor.
This is your capstone. In Task A, you build a complete go-to-market plan for a new Eat Better product or expansion. First, choose a project track.
Your proposal covers six pillars, from the product and its pricing to distribution, the launch campaign and a basic financial plan.
Build it in any tool you like, and check the rubric so you know exactly what a great proposal looks like.
In Task B, you design an online storefront for the product you planned in Task A. Pick the kind of storefront you want to build.
A great storefront has four parts: original packaging and product images, clear product listings with prices, an easy cart and checkout, and Eat Better's look and feel.
Choose a tool, then use the checklist to make sure everything is ready before you submit.
